01.note: A group of ice plant dealers took turns baking for one another, one each day. One day the others told one of them to go and bake for them, and he asked them to look after his cloak. Before he came back they were careless with it and it was stolen. Rav Pappa ruled that they had to pay for it. The Rabbis objected that this was negligence while the owner was working for them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. In the end it came out that at that very time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer, not baking.
01.why: The Gemara has just discussed the rule that a guardian who is in the owner's service, or has the owner in his, is exempt. This case tests that rule; right after it the Gemara asks why Rav Pappa was embarrassed and retells the case so that it fits both views of the law.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who heard the case and made the dealers pay for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: A group of traders in a particular plant who shared their baking, each taking a turn.
A case where a guardian is careless while the owner of the item is working for him. One view in the Gemara says the guardian is then exempt from paying.

02.note: This is the Gemara's second telling of the stolen cloak. Here the baker took on a turn that was not his, and asked the others to guard his cloak as his payment. Before he came back it was stolen. Rav Pappa made them pay. The Sages said this was guarding while the owner was with them, and Rav Pappa was embarrassed. In the end it came out that at that time the cloak's owner had been drinking beer.
02.why: The Gemara asked why Rav Pappa would be embarrassed if a careless guardian must pay even while the owner works for him. It retells the case so the dealers were paid guardians, and the Sages' objection is about the owner's presence rather than negligence.

people.name: Rav Pappa
people.about: The Sage who made the guardians pay for the stolen cloak.

terms.meaning: When the owner of an item is working for the guardian at the time, the guardian is not liable for what happens to it.

02.flag: The story starts mid-retelling: the setup of this version (it was not his turn, guard my cloak as payment) sits in the segment before it.

03.note: Two men were travelling, one tall and one short. The tall one rode a donkey and had a sheet; the short one walked, wrapped in a woolen cloak. At a river, the short man put his cloak on the donkey to keep it dry, took the tall man's sheet and covered himself with it, and the water washed the sheet away. The tall man came before Rava, who made the short man pay. The Rabbis objected that this was borrowing with the owner present, and Rava was embarrassed. In the end it came out that the short man had taken the sheet without the tall man knowing and put it back without his knowing.
03.why: It follows the case of Rav Pappa and the cloak, with the same shape: a ruling challenged on the rule that a borrower or guardian is exempt when the owner is with him, and then vindicated by a fact that came out later.

people.name: Rava
people.about: The Sage who made the short man pay for the lost sheet.

terms.meaning: When the owner of a borrowed item is with the borrower or working for him at the time, the borrower is not liable for loss. Taking without permission is not borrowing at all.

04.note: A man rented his donkey to another and told him: do not take the Nehar Pekod road, where there is water; take the Neresh road, where there is none. The renter took the Nehar Pekod road and the donkey died. When he came back he said: yes, I went by Nehar Pekod, but there was no water there.
04.why: Rava then rules the renter is believed, since he could have lied and said he took the other road; Abaye answers that this argument does not work where witnesses can be brought to show whether there was water.

terms.meaning: Two routes the owner names: the Nehar Pekod road has water along it, which he fears, and the Neresh road does not.

05.note: Some porters Rabba bar bar Hanan had hired broke a barrel of his wine, and he took their cloaks. They went and told Rav, who told him to give back their cloaks. Rabba bar bar Hanan asked whether that was the law, and Rav said yes, quoting Proverbs: "That you may walk in the way of good men." He returned the cloaks. The porters then said they were poor, had worked all day, were hungry and had nothing. Rav told him to pay their wages. Asked again if that was the law, Rav said yes: "And keep the paths of the righteous."
05.why: The Gemara has been discussing when carriers who break what they carry must pay, including Rav Hiyya bar Yosef's decree of half payment. Here Rav asks the employer to go beyond what the law strictly demands.

people.name: Rabba bar bar Hanan
people.about: The employer whose wine barrel the porters broke, and who took their cloaks.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage the porters went to, who told Rabba bar bar Hanan to return their cloaks and pay them.

terms.meaning: Jewish law. Rabba bar bar Hanan asks whether Rav's instruction is what the law requires.

06.note: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, met an officer who arrested thieves and asked how he could tell them, since they hide like beasts; perhaps he took the righteous and left the wicked. The officer said it was the king's order. Rabbi Elazar taught him a test: a man dozing over his wine at the fourth hour who is not a scholar or a worker up early is a thief. The palace heard, and made Rabbi Elazar do the job himself. Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha called him vinegar, son of wine. When a laundryman insulted him, Rabbi Elazar had him arrested; he later tried to ransom him and failed, and wept under the gallows. Told the man had sinned gravely, he rejoiced, yet was not at peace until his belly was cut open and the fat did not rot in the sun.
06.why: The Gemara has just read Psalms 104:20, "all the beasts of the forest creep forth," as the wicked of this world. The story opens with that verse and turns on rising early, a theme of the surrounding discussion about laborers' hours.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who advised an officer how to catch thieves and was then made to arrest them himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha
people.about: A Sage who rebuked Rabbi Elazar for handing Jews over to be executed.

terms.meaning: An insult: a bad son of a good father, as vinegar is spoiled wine.
The hottest summer months in the Jewish calendar.
The Day of Atonement, the holiest day of the Jewish year.

07.note: Like Rabbi Elazar, Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, came to be arresting thieves for the government. Elijah the prophet met him and asked: until when will you hand over the people of our God to be executed? Rabbi Yishmael answered that it was the king's order. Elijah told him: your father fled to Asia; you flee to Laodicea. The text does not say what he did.
07.why: It comes straight after the story of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, as a matching case of a Sage serving the Roman authorities as a thief-catcher, this time rebuked by Elijah.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: A Sage who, like Rabbi Elazar, arrested thieves on the king's orders.

people.name: Elijah
people.about: The prophet, who rebuked Rabbi Yishmael and told him to flee.

terms.meaning: A city Elijah names as a place to flee to, as Rabbi Yishmael's father had fled to Asia.

08.note: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei, and Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, were so fat that when they stood facing each other a pair of oxen could pass between them without touching them. A Roman noblewoman told them their children could not be theirs. They answered that their wives' bellies were bigger than theirs; she said that made it even less likely. Other versions give their answer as a verse, "For as the man is, so is his strength," or the saying "Love compresses the flesh."
08.why: Having told how both Sages served as thief-catchers, the Gemara turns to their bodies; afterward it asks why they answered so foolish a question at all, and says it was to protect their children's good name.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: One of the two very fat Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The other very fat Sage.

terms.meaning: A Roman noblewoman.

09.note: Rabbi Yohanan used to sit by the entrance to the ritual bath, saying that when Jewish women came up from immersing they should meet him, so they would have children as beautiful and as learned in Torah as he was. The Rabbis asked whether he was not afraid of the evil eye. He answered that he came from the descendants of Joseph, over whom the evil eye has no power, citing a verse about Joseph as read by Rabbi Abbahu.
09.why: The Gemara has been describing Rabbi Yohanan's beauty, and has just explained why he is missing from a list of beautiful men: he had no beard. This story continues that theme.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: A Sage famed for his beauty, who sat by the ritual bath so women would see him.

people.name: Rabbi Abbahu
people.about: A Sage whose reading of a verse about Joseph Rabbi Yohanan quotes.

people.name: Joseph
people.about: The biblical son of Jacob, from whom Rabbi Yohanan says he descends.

terms.meaning: A pool where a woman immerses after menstruation before she and her husband resume relations.
The belief that envious looks from others can cause harm.

10.note: Reish Lakish, a bandit, leapt into the Jordan after Rabbi Yohanan, who promised him his sister if he took up Torah. He did, and became a great scholar. Years later Rabbi Yohanan taunted him about knowing weapons as a bandit; hurt, Reish Lakish fell ill and died, and Rabbi Yohanan grieved until he lost his mind and died. The Gemara then returns to Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, who took suffering on himself, was blessed with wealth and ruled boldly, and asked to be laid in his attic when he died. His body stayed uncorrupted there for years, and a voice from the attic judged cases. When the Rabbis learned he was unburied, they brought him to his father's cave, where a serpent blocking the entrance opened to let the son in beside his father.
10.why: The Gemara has been discussing Rabbi Yohanan's beauty; the Jordan story begins there. It then picks up the unfinished story of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, to show that despite the proof of his righteousness he still did not trust himself.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who drew Reish Lakish to Torah, gave him his sister, and grieved for him to death.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A bandit leader who became a great scholar and Rabbi Yohanan's study partner; also called Rabbi Shimon ben Lakish.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar ben Pedat
people.about: A Sage sent to comfort Rabbi Yohanan, who only agreed with him.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A Sage who took suffering on himself; his body lay unburied in his attic for years.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's father, who in one version appeared in a dream asking for his son.

terms.term: under the wings of the Divine Presence
terms.meaning: Close to God; Rabbi Yohanan's way of saying he brought Reish Lakish into Jewish life and learning.
A teaching of the early Sages that was not included in the Mishna, the first written code of Jewish law.
Here, ruling that a blood stain was not menstrual, so the woman was permitted to her husband.
The town where Rabbi Elazar's body lay, whose people did not want it moved.

10.flag: Combines two stories: Rabbi Yohanan and Reish Lakish, then the return to Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, from his afflictions to his burial; each could stand alone.

11.note: When Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha sat on benches, the young Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) sat before them on the ground. They asked and answered so well that the elders gave them benches. Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel asked that his son be taken down, fearing for him, and Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha asked whether the fatherless one should be left to die, so both were taken down. Rabbi Elazar was offended that he had been treated as Rabbi's equal, and from then on cut down Rabbi's arguments before he could make them. Rabbi was hurt and told his father, who said: he is a lion son of a lion, and you are a lion son of a fox.
11.why: Rabbi Elazar's widow told Rabbi he was not greater than her husband in Torah or deeds; the Gemara asks what showed his greater Torah, and this story is the answer. It also explains Rabbi's later saying about three modest people.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: A brilliant young scholar, son of Rabbi Shimon, whose father had died.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, son of Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel, Rabbi Elazar's young study companion.

people.name: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel
people.about: Rabbi's father, a leading Sage, who asked that his son not be raised up.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Korha
people.about: A leading Sage who argued that Rabbi Elazar should be protected too.

terms.meaning: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel's name for his only son, whom he feared would be harmed by too much honor too young.

terms.term: a lion son of a fox
terms.meaning: A great man whose father was lesser; Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel humbly says this of himself.

11.flag: The story ends mid-sentence: Rabbi's list of three modest people ("Father, ...") is completed in the next segment.

12.note: When Rabbi (Yehuda HaNasi) heard what Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, had gained through suffering, he said: afflictions are precious. He took thirteen years of afflictions upon himself: six years of kidney stones and seven of scurvy, or, some say, seven of kidney stones and six of scurvy.
12.why: Rabbi Elazar's widow told Rabbi that her husband was greater in deeds because he accepted afflictions. Here Rabbi responds by taking suffering on himself; the Gemara goes on to say his suffering was still not equal to Rabbi Elazar's.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who took years of suffering upon himself.

terms.meaning: Suffering that a person accepts on himself, believed to atone for sin and bring a person closer to God.

13.note: A calf being led to slaughter ran and hid its head in the corner of Rabbi's garment, weeping. He told it: go, this is what you were created for. In Heaven they said: since he had no compassion, let afflictions come upon him. Years later his maidservant was sweeping the house and sweeping out some young weasels. Rabbi told her to leave them, quoting "His mercies are over all His works." Heaven said: since he is compassionate, we will be compassionate to him, and his suffering ended.
13.why: The Gemara has just said that Rabbi Elazar's afflictions came and went out of love, while Rabbi's came and went because of incidents. This story tells those two incidents.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, whose suffering began and ended with how he treated animals.

14.note: Rabbi came to the town of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon, and asked if that righteous man had a son. They said he did, and that any prostitute hired for two coins hired him for eight. Rabbi brought him back, ordained him and gave him to his uncle, Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya, to teach. Every day the young man said he was going back to his town, until his uncle shamed him and he vowed to stay. Grown into a scholar, he sat in Rabbi's academy, and Rabbi knew his father's voice in his. Rabbi applied to him and his uncle the verse "The fruit of the righteous is a tree of life; and he that is wise wins souls." When this Rabbi Yosei died, the serpent at his father's cave would not open for him, and people thought his father was greater.
14.why: It continues the account of Rabbi and Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon. The serpent echoes Rabbi Elazar's own burial, and the Divine Voice that follows says the son was not lesser, he had not suffered in the cave as his father had.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who rescued Rabbi Elazar's son and had him taught.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Elazar, son of Rabbi Shimon
people.about: Rabbi Elazar's wayward son, who became a scholar.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Isi ben Lakonya
people.about: The young man's uncle, his mother's brother, who taught him Torah.

terms.meaning: Gave him the title Rabbi, here as a way to draw him into a life of learning.
A mark of the honor given to someone ordained as a Sage.

15.note: Rabbi came to the town of Rabbi Tarfon and asked whether that righteous man, who used to swear by the lives of his children, had a son. They said he had no son but had a grandson through his daughter, whom any prostitute hired for two coins hired for eight. They brought him to Rabbi, who said: if you repent, I will give you my daughter. He repented. Some say he married her and then divorced her; others say he never married her, so no one could say he repented for her sake.
15.why: It is told as a match to Rabbi rescuing Rabbi Elazar's son. The Gemara then asks why Rabbi took such trouble over wayward sons, and answers that whoever teaches Torah to another's son earns a seat in the heavenly academy.

people.name: Rabbi
people.about: Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi, who offered his daughter to bring the young man back.

people.name: Rabbi Tarfon
people.about: A righteous Sage who used to swear by the lives of his children; his daughter's son had gone astray.

16.note: Rav Yosef fasted forty fasts, and in a dream was read the verse "My words shall not depart out of your mouth." He fasted forty more and was read "...nor out of the mouth of your seed." He fasted again and was read the end of the verse, "...nor out of the mouth of your seed's seed." He said: from now on I do not need to fast, the Torah returns to its lodging.
16.why: Rabbi Yohanan has just taught that when three generations are Torah scholars the Torah will never leave the family, from Isaiah 59:21. Rav Yosef fasts until he is promised exactly that.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: A Sage who fasted so that Torah would stay in his family.

terms.term: the Torah returns to its lodging
terms.meaning: A saying that after three generations of scholars, Torah learning keeps coming back to that family as to its home.

17.note: When Rabbi Zeira moved up to the Land of Israel, he fasted a hundred fasts to forget the Babylonian way of studying, so it would not get in his way. He fasted another hundred so that Rabbi Elazar would not die in his lifetime and leave the burden of public affairs to him. He fasted another hundred so that the fire of Gehenna would have no power over him.
17.why: It is told as a match to Rav Yosef's fasts, another Sage fasting for something tied to his Torah learning.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who moved from Babylonia to the Land of Israel.

people.name: Rabbi Elazar
people.about: A Sage whose long life, Rabbi Zeira hoped, would keep public duties away from him.

terms.meaning: The place where the wicked are punished after death, often pictured as fire.

18.note: Every thirty days Rabbi Zeira tested himself: he would heat an oven, climb in and sit inside, and the fire did not touch him. One day the Sages cast the evil eye on him and his legs were singed. From then on they called him "the short one with singed legs."
18.why: It follows Rabbi Zeira's fasts so that the fire of Gehenna would not touch him; the oven was how he checked that the fasts still held.

people.name: Rabbi Zeira
people.about: A Sage who had fasted that fire would not harm him, and tested it in an oven.

terms.meaning: The belief that envious looks from others can cause harm.

19.note: Reish Lakish was marking the burial caves of the Sages. When he reached the cave of Rabbi Hiyya, it was hidden from him. Upset, he said: Master of the Universe, did I not analyze the Torah as he did? A Divine Voice answered: you analyzed Torah as he did, but you did not spread Torah as he did.
19.why: The discussion has been about the greatness of Sages and of those who teach Torah. The story leads into Rabbi Hiyya's own account of how he made sure the Torah would not be forgotten.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: A Sage who was marking the graves of earlier Sages.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage whose grave Reish Lakish could not find.

terms.meaning: A voice from Heaven that speaks in Talmud stories to settle a question.

20.note: Whenever Rabbi Hanina and Rabbi Hiyya argued, Rabbi Hanina would say: are you arguing with me? If the Torah were forgotten from Israel, I could restore it by my reasoning. Rabbi Hiyya answered: are you arguing with me? I act so that the Torah will not be forgotten from Israel.
20.why: It follows the Divine Voice telling Reish Lakish that Rabbi Hiyya spread Torah more than others. Rabbi Hiyya goes on to describe how he did it.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: A Sage who boasted he could restore the Torah by his reasoning.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who said he worked to keep the Torah from being forgotten.

20.flag: Stops mid-exchange: Rabbi Hiyya's explanation of what he does (flax, deer, teaching children) is in the next segment.
